recipe.history:
The holiday turkey at the center of American Christmas and Thanksgiving tables is the descendant of the wild turkey — Meleagris gallopavo — native to North America, domesticated by indigenous Mesoamerican civilizations as early as 800 BCE. The Aztecs and other Mesoamerican peoples domesticated the bird primarily for its feathers and as a ritual animal before it became a food source, and Spanish conquistadors brought domesticated turkeys back to Europe in the sixteenth century, where they spread rapidly through France, England, and the rest of the continent. By the time European settlers arrived in North America, the turkey they found in the wild was already a familiar species to them through its domesticated European relatives. Turkey became the centerpiece of American holiday tradition partly by accident and partly through the romanticized mythology of the Pilgrim harvest feast, but its dominance on the Christmas table is a relatively recent development — beef and pork held that position in England and early America for centuries before the turkey's symbolic weight solidified its holiday status. Cranberry sauce, the essential accompaniment, draws on indigenous North American tradition: Native American peoples of the Northeast had long used wild cranberries — Vaccinium macrocarpon, native to the bogs of New England and the Great Lakes — for food, medicine, and dye, and it was indigenous people who introduced European settlers to the tart red berry that would become inseparable from the roast turkey tradition.

The post-Christmas leftover sandwich is one of the great traditions of American home cooking: the day-after-Christmas turkey sandwich, constructed from whatever remains after the feast, is for many families as anticipated as the feast itself. The combination of turkey, cranberry sauce, stuffing, and gravy in a single construction is a purely American invention — a dish that exists only in the context of abundance and the creative recycling of festive excess. When this combination migrates to a burger context — placed on a beef patty and tucked into a pretzel roll — it transforms from a leftover sandwich into a deliberate composition, each element chosen and placed rather than improvised from what remains. The Brie, which carries its own French holiday tradition, adds a layer of richness and brine-edged creaminess that bridges the savory turkey and gravy with the sweet-tart cranberry, creating a burger that tastes like Christmas without tasting like leftovers.

Every year after Christmas, without fail, I make the same thing for lunch on the twenty-sixth: I take whatever is left of the turkey, whatever gravy remains in the pan, the cranberry sauce if any survived the holiday, and whatever bread is available, and I build the most extravagant sandwich I can. The discipline of the actual Christmas table — where everything is served in its correct vessel and consumed in its proper order — is gone, and what takes its place is the freedom of improvisation. One year I had a ripe Brie that I had been saving and I sliced it onto the turkey and let the gravy melt it and I stood at the kitchen counter eating that sandwich and thinking that it was possibly better than the original meal had been. The stuffing croutons in this recipe are my attempt to preserve the stuffing's flavor and crunch in a form that works on a burger — toasted small cubes of herb-stuffed bread that stay crispy under the gravy long enough to matter.

Putting holiday leftovers on a beef patty is an act of cheerful irreverence, and irreverence requires confidence. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is a confident patty — it shows up pink and assertive, juicy and fat-rich, unwilling to be overwhelmed by the gravy or the cranberry or the Brie. It insists on being part of the celebration rather than merely a vehicle for toppings. A well-done patty in this context would disappear under the gravy, dry and gray, indistinguishable from the stuffing. Medium rare keeps the beef present at the table, a full participant in the post-Christmas abundance. Pull it at 130 to 135. Rest it. Let the holidays begin again.
ingredients: 1 lb boneless turkey breast or turkey thigh
Note: Leftover roasted Christmas turkey is ideal; if roasting fresh, roast at 375°F for 25 to 30 minutes until internal temperature reaches 165°F. Slice or pull into pieces.
Salt and black pepper to taste
3 cups day-old rustic bread, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
4 oz Brie cheese, rind removed, cut into slices
instructions: 1. Make the cranberry sauce: Combine cranberries, sugar, orange juice, orange zest, cinnamon, and salt in a small saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 10 to 12 minutes until the cranberries burst and the sauce thickens to a jammy consistency. Remove from heat and let cool. Refrigerate until needed. This can be made days ahead.

2. Make the stuffing croutons: Preheat oven to 375°F. Heat butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté celery and onion until softened, about 5 minutes. Add thyme and sage, cook 1 minute. Add bread cubes and toss to coat in the butter and vegetable mixture. Drizzle chicken stock over the bread, just enough to moisten slightly without soaking. Spread on a parchment-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Bake 15 to 20 minutes until golden, crisp on the outside, and slightly soft inside. Set aside.

3. Make the herb turkey gravy: Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook 1 to 2 minutes until the roux turns light golden and smells nutty. Gradually whisk in stock, ensuring no lumps. Add thyme and sage. Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until thickened to a pourable but coating consistency. Add cream if using. Season with salt and pepper. Keep warm over low heat.

4. Prepare the turkey: If roasting fresh, toss turkey breast or thigh with olive oil, salt, pepper, thyme, sage, and garlic powder. Roast at 375°F until internal temperature reaches 165°F, about 25 to 30 minutes for a breast portion. Let rest 10 minutes, then slice or pull into pieces. If using leftover roasted turkey, warm the slices gently in a covered skillet with a splash of stock.

5. Make the pretzel rolls: Combine warm water, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes. Add salt and softened butter. Add flour one cup at a time with the dough hook on low. Increase to medium and knead 7 to 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise at room temperature 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.

6. Divide dough into 4 portions. Shape into tight balls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and proof 30 to 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 425°F. Bring baking soda water to a boil. Boil each roll 30 seconds per side. Return to baking sheet, brush with egg wash, score tops, sprinkle with pretzel salt. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until deep mahogany. Cool briefly.

7. Form the patties: Mix dried thyme gently into the ground beef. Divide into 4 portions. Form into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat. Lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up for 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip once, lay Brie slices over each patty, and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F and Brie begins to melt. Remove from heat, tent with foil, and rest 3 minutes.
9. Split pretzel rolls and toast cut-side down in butter in the skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

10. Assemble the burgers: Spread cranberry sauce generously on both cut sides of the pretzel roll. Place the rested patty with melted Brie on the bottom bun. Layer sliced or pulled turkey on top of the patty. Spoon warm gravy over the turkey, letting it flow down the sides. Scatter a generous handful of stuffing croutons over the gravy. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately with additional cranberry sauce and gravy on the side.
